comment: Chemistry exam-day facts and the technique rules distilled from the 2021-2025 mark schemes and teacher commentary (see scratchpad notes). No formula sheet exists for chemistry — the periodic table is the only thing given, so the 'formulaSheet' block explains that and lists what must be memorised instead.

examDay.dateText: No exam date yet — GCSE summer 2027
bring: Sharp pencil and rubber for graphs and diagrams
provided: A copy of the Periodic Table — atomic numbers and relative atomic masses for every element. Nothing else is given: every equation and definition must be memorised.
rules: One minute per mark, roughly. A 13-mark question deserves 13 minutes, not 25.
Answer every question. A blank scores zero; a partial answer often scores something.

Show every step in calculations. A correct final answer with no working scores full marks, but a wrong answer with no working scores zero — the moles step is almost always the first mark, and error-carried-forward protects the rest.
Read what the answer line demands before calculating: the unit, the significant figures, standard form. In 2024 marks were lost for ignoring '2 significant figures' printed in the question.
Use accurate scientific terminology — it is printed on the front page and the schemes enforce it: ion not atom, molecular formula not chemical formula, effervescence not fizzing-ish.
Chemical formulae are case-sensitive: HBr not HBR, NaCl not NACL. Spelling of names must be exact (propane, not 'triane').

formulaSheet.note: There is no formula sheet in chemistry — only the Periodic Table is provided. These are the relationships that must be in your head; they are also flashcards in the Chemical Calculations module.

given.words: percentage of an element by mass

techniqueRules.rule: It is the ION that gains or loses electrons at an electrode — never the metal.
techniqueRules.detail: 2023: "Huge number wrote magnesium gains electrons. This is not true! The magnesium ION gains electrons, not the magnesium!!" Same at the anode: bromide IONS lose electrons, not bromine.

techniqueRules.rule: Redox answers name the whole compound: iron(III) OXIDE is reduced, oxygen is removed from calcium PHOSPHATE.
techniqueRules.detail: 2024: many said 'iron was reduced' (iron is the product) or that oxygen was removed from 'the calcium'. Name the full compound the oxygen leaves.

techniqueRules.rule: The role of carbon: reducing agent, REMOVES oxygen — not 'reacts with' or 'displaces' it.
techniqueRules.detail: Asked in 2024 AND 2025, fluffed both years. Two marks: (1) carbon is the reducing agent; (2) it removes oxygen from [named compound].

techniqueRules.rule: Ionic solids don't conduct because the IONS can't move — never mention electrons; giant structures have no molecules.
techniqueRules.detail: Electron-based answers for ionic conduction score zero. 'Molecules of sodium chloride/graphite' is a category error the schemes reject.

techniqueRules.rule: Boiling a simple molecular substance overcomes weak intermolecular forces BETWEEN MOLECULES — covalent bonds never break.
techniqueRules.detail: 2021: "any reference to breaking covalent or ionic bonds scores 0/2." And never put intermolecular forces inside graphite or any giant structure — that cancels marks too (2022).

techniqueRules.rule: Ionic melting point: giant ionic lattice · strong attraction between oppositely charged ions · lots of energy. No covalent words.
techniqueRules.detail: 2025: any mention of covalent bonds, molecules or IMF in the ionic melting-point answer scored 0/3.

techniqueRules.rule: A covalent bond: shared pair attracted to the NUCLEI of BOTH atoms — plural.
techniqueRules.detail: 2021 and 2022 both refused the mark for 'attracted to the nucleus'.

techniqueRules.rule: Ionic bonding stories count electrons: magnesium loses TWO, oxygen gains TWO.
techniqueRules.detail: 2023: 'electrons moved from magnesium to oxygen' without the number scored neither mark.

techniqueRules.rule: Collision theory needs FREQUENCY: more collisions per unit time / more frequent — 'more chance of colliding' scores nothing.
techniqueRules.detail: Every year. 2025 additionally demanded 'successful' linked to time: more SUCCESSFUL collisions per unit time.

techniqueRules.rule: Concentration and surface-area answers never mention energy; temperature answers must have BOTH more-energetic collisions and a greater proportion successful.
techniqueRules.detail: 2024 capped concentration-with-kinetic-energy answers at 1 of 3. 2023 wanted 'greater proportion of collisions are successful' as its own point, separate from frequency.

techniqueRules.rule: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway WITH a lower activation energy — both halves or a mark is lost.
techniqueRules.detail: 2025: "a lot of students mentioned lowering activation energy so could not score M2" — the pathway is the mechanism, the lower Ea its property.

techniqueRules.rule: Rate at a time = the gradient of a TANGENT at that time, with the unit the axes demand (cm³/min, g/s).
techniqueRules.detail: 2022: the average-rate answer scored 1 of 3. 2025: 'm is meters!' — min for minutes, cm³ not cm.

techniqueRules.rule: Heat a salt solution only to the CRYSTALLISATION POINT, then cool — heating to dryness caps the answer at 1 mark.
techniqueRules.detail: 2024 and 2025 both. Dryness wrecks hydrated crystals: the water of crystallisation is driven off.

techniqueRules.rule: A precipitate is the RESIDUE: filter, wash the residue with distilled water, dry gently — never wash the filtrate, never Bunsen-dry.
techniqueRules.detail: 2023: "the salt you want is the residue." 2022 rejected direct heating for drying. Soluble-salt methods described for a precipitation score 1 mark at most.

techniqueRules.rule: You cannot filter out a soluble salt — sodium salts are ALWAYS soluble.
techniqueRules.detail: 2025: "'filtering out the sodium sulfate' scores 0 — it is not a precipitate." Check the solubility rules before choosing a method.

techniqueRules.rule: Excess solid is used SO THAT ALL THE ACID REACTS — then filtered off.
techniqueRules.detail: The reason is a one-mark answer on its own (2024). 'To make more salt' misses the point.

techniqueRules.rule: Heating to constant mass proves the change is complete — reheat, cool, reweigh until the mass stops changing.
techniqueRules.detail: The improve-the-accuracy answer for every crucible practical (2022, 2024). If x in a hydrate comes out low: not heated long enough, water remains.

techniqueRules.rule: 'Fair test' scores nothing — name the variables kept constant.
techniqueRules.detail: Same volume and concentration of acid, same mass of catalyst, same temperature: the named list is the mark.

techniqueRules.rule: An observation is what you SEE: effervescence, a blue precipitate forms, the ribbon disappears — not the name of a gas.
techniqueRules.detail: 2023: 'to score the mark you had to state what you would see.' 'Hydrogen is given off' is ignored; extra wrong observations are penalised.

techniqueRules.rule: Gas tests: LIT splint → squeaky pop = hydrogen · GLOWING splint relights = oxygen · damp litmus bleached = chlorine · limewater milky = CO₂.
techniqueRules.detail: 2024 rejected the glowing splint for hydrogen. Lit and glowing are different tests.

techniqueRules.rule: State symbols follow where the substance actually is: dissolved salts and acids (aq), water (l), precipitates (s).
techniqueRules.detail: 2024: many wrote zinc nitrate as (s) or (l) — it is a soluble salt in solution, (aq).

techniqueRules.rule: Empirical formulae: divide mass or % by the RELATIVE ATOMIC MASS — atomic numbers or upside-down fractions score 0/3.
techniqueRules.detail: 2021's scheme says exactly that. And never round 1.33 to 1 — multiply up (×3) to whole numbers.

techniqueRules.rule: Large answers in standard form; obey a stated significant-figure count.
techniqueRules.detail: 2022/2023 gave a dedicated mark for 4.8 × 10⁶. 2024: "did not read the question so did not leave the final answer to 2 sf."

techniqueRules.rule: % yield = actual MASS ÷ theoretical MASS × 100 — convert expected moles to grams first.
techniqueRules.detail: 2025 rejected actual-mass ÷ moles. Excess questions likewise compare MOLES needed with moles available, never grams.

techniqueRules.rule: Show construction lines on every graph reading, and draw single smooth best-fit lines with a sharp pencil.
techniqueRules.detail: 2023/2024/2025 all marked the working lines. 2023: "sloppy graphs — blunt pencils, sketchy feathery lines" were penalised; read the curve the question names.

techniqueRules.rule: Balance with coefficients only — never edit a formula — and actually write the balancing numbers.
techniqueRules.detail: 2024: "many got close but did not include balancing numbers." Formulae first, then balance, then recount every element.

techniqueRules.rule: H₂ N₂ O₂ F₂ Cl₂ Br₂ I₂ — elemental halogens and gases are diatomic, in half-equations too.
techniqueRules.detail: 2023: "as usual, many forgot chlorine was diatomic… fascinating variations including Cl⁺ and Cl₃."

techniqueRules.rule: The anode half-equation in solution starts from water: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ — there are no O²⁻ ions in a solution.
techniqueRules.detail: 2023's most common wrong answer was 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻. The alternative 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ is also accepted.

techniqueRules.rule: Pollution chains need every link: fuel CONTAINS sulfur → burns to SO₂ → acid rain. Skipping the first link forfeits the last.
techniqueRules.detail: 2025: the acid-rain mark was dependent on the earlier ones — "lots got 0". Greenhouse gases belong to a different question.

techniqueRules.rule: Fractional distillation, 4 marks, verbatim: heated/vaporised · vapours RISE · hotter at the bottom · each vapour CONDENSES where the column is cooler than its boiling point.
techniqueRules.detail: Asked three years running (2023, 2024, 2025). The lost marks are 'rise' and tying condensation to the boiling point.

techniqueRules.rule: 'Explain why X is oxidised' wants the definition applied: it GAINS OXYGEN / the ions LOSE ELECTRONS — not just the product's name.
techniqueRules.detail: 2021: 'it forms SO₂' did not score; 'the sulfur gains oxygen' did.

diagramChecklists.title: Dot-and-cross diagram (covalent)
diagramChecklists.note: 2-mark pattern: M1 the bonding pairs, M2 everything else exactly right. Any mix of dots and crosses is fine.
items: Right number of shared pairs between the right atoms (N₂ needs six shared electrons)
Every lone pair drawn — count each atom's outer electrons and check they are all present
Outer shells only, unless the question says otherwise
Shared electrons sit inside the overlap; one from each atom (one dot + one cross per pair)

diagramChecklists.title: Displayed formula
diagramChecklists.note: Displayed means every atom AND every bond drawn.
items: All C–H bonds shown — a –CH₃ written as a lump is rejected
Every carbon has exactly four bonds
Count the atoms at the end and check them against the molecular formula
For isomers: confirm the two drawings are genuinely different structures, not one molecule bent

diagramChecklists.title: Graph work (rates and solubility)
diagramChecklists.note: The commentary's biggest recurring complaint. Sharp pencil.
items: Points plotted exact to the nearest gridline, marked with a clear ×
One single smooth best-fit line — no sketchy/feathery strokes; even spread of points either side
Curve clearly through the origin when the data starts there; plateau exactly level
Construction lines drawn and left visible for every value read off the graph
Tangent (rates): touches the curve at the stated time only, big triangle, unit from the axes
Read the curve the question names — not the nearest one

diagramChecklists.title: Salt preparation method (before writing)
diagramChecklists.note: Thirty seconds of method choice saves four marks.
items: Checked the solubility rules for the TARGET salt first
Insoluble target → mix two solutions, filter, wash the RESIDUE, dry gently
Soluble target + insoluble partner → excess solid, filter, heat filtrate to crystallisation point only
Soluble target + both reactants soluble → titration route
No heating to dryness anywhere; drying method named (filter paper / warm oven / warm place)
